questions.question: What are the construction characteristics of thee basic types of fuel tanks?
questions.idealAnswer: The three types of tanks are rigid, bladder, and integral tank. The rigid tank is usually made of aluminum or stainless steel and is riveted and has welded seams to prevent leaks. Rigid tanks are removable. Some modern rigid tanks are made from composite materials. Bladder tanks are made from a reinforced flexible material. Bladder tanks are also removable. Bladder tanks are repairable by patching and other techniques in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions. Integral tanks are formed as part of the wing or part of the fuselage and is sealed with a fuel resistant two part sealant to prevent leaks. A integral tank is not removable as it is part of the main structure of the aircraft. They are repairable by draining, cleaning, and resealing. All fuel tanks regardless of their construction must have means for venting, have a sump located at the lowest point where water and sediment can collect and be drained out. Many tanks have baffles to prevent the rapid movement of fuel during flight maneuvers and scuppers to drain away any spilled fuel at fill port areas.

questions.question: What are some general rules for installation and routing of fuel lines on an aircraft?
questions.idealAnswer: Hoses should be installed without twisting, and separation should be observed between all fuel hoses/ lines and electrical wiring. All fuel lines and hoses should be installed below the electrical wiring. All metal fuel lines and components need to be electrically bonded and grounded to the aircraft structure. Special bonded cushion clamps should be used to secure rigid fuel lines in place. All fuel lines should be supported so that there is no strain on the fittings. Specific intervals for clamping are required when securing lines depending on their diameter. Never draw two lines fittings together by threading A wrench should be used only when tightening. A straight length of rigid line should not be made between two components or rigidly mounted to the airframe. A small bend should be made to absorb any strain from vibration or expansion and contraction due to temperature changes.

questions.question: On many aircraft fuel systems, what is done to ensure positive fuel flow to the engines?
questions.idealAnswer: If the aircraft has fuel tanks located above the carburetor (high wing) gravity is used to deliver the fuel to the engine. Vented fuel tanks enable the atmospheric pressure to remain on the fuel load forcing it through the fuel lines to the carburetor. Shifting fuel, high temperatures, and reduced atmospheric pressure as the aircraft gains altitude are concerns to avoid vapor lock. On low wing aircraft boost pumps are used, these boost pumps are located inside the fuel tank or at the tank outlet. Boost pumps force the fuel under pressure through the lines leading to metering devices to ensure no interruption of fuel flow. Some light aircraft employ pumps that pull the fuel from the tanks in lieu of tank mounted boost pumps.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a fuel jettison system and what are some characteristics of a typical fuel jettison system?
questions.idealAnswer: If an aircraft's design landing weight is less than that of maximum take off weight, a situation could occur in which a landing is desired before sufficient fuel has burned off to lighten the aircraft to or below the acceptable landing weight. Fuel jettisoning systems are required in these aircraft so that the fuel can be jettisoned in flight to avoid structural damage caused by landing the aircraft when it is to heavy. Characteristics of a fuel jettison systems are, the rate of fuel jettisoning as well as the various attitudes, speeds, and configurations of the aircraft are taken into consideration. The fuel must discharge clear of any part of the aircraft. The discharge of the fuel must not affect the controllability of the aircraft. There must be enough redundancy so that the failure of a single component does not prevent the fuel from being jettisoned. Also, the process of jettisoning fuel must be able to be controlled by a valve and stopped if desired. The amount of fuel able to be jettisoned is also controlled.
